rows.claim: D-136: a noisy frame allocates a fresh ring lazily, once, at the writer's next emission after a drain.
rows.evidence: probe:62 (allocations per `report_cell!` call, emissions 1-16: 144, 192, 240, 240, 320, 320, 352, 352, 480, 496, 512, 544, 560, 560, 576, 608 bytes); src/dataplane.jl:141-150 (`DiagBatch(push!(copy(current.ring), occurrence), …)` on every append)
rows.note: Every append below capacity copies the whole ring, because the CAS swaps immutable `DiagBatch` values. Spec §11.8 (spec.md:9661-9664) states the lazy-fresh-ring rule as well. The cost lands on the writer's task, outside the stepping loop's invariant.
rows.fix: Docs: "a noisy frame allocates on the writer's task at each emission: below capacity the CAS appends by copying the ring, so the n-th value of a frame copies n entries." Code alternative: let the writer own a fresh ring after each drain and append to it in place, swapping by identity.

rows.claim: D-136: the worst case per writer per boundary is one ring of 16, and everything past it is an integer increment.
rows.evidence: probe:62 (16 ring copies of growing size, about 6 KB in a frame, then 32 bytes for each suppressed emission past capacity); src/dataplane.jl:141-150
rows.note: The bound holds in entry count but not in allocation. Past capacity each emission builds a new `DiagBatch` for the CAS, at 32 bytes measured. Spec §11.8 (spec.md:9666-9667) states the same bound.
rows.fix: Docs: "The worst case per writer per frame is sixteen ring copies of up to sixteen values, then one small batch record for each emission past capacity." Or code: count past-capacity emissions with an atomic counter field rather than a rebuilt batch.

- 13 are drift that the entry's own annotation already records, so they need no rewrite: 023, 024, 025, 044, 046, 080, 089, 112, 132, 134 and 184.

This contradicts D-136's bound and spec §11.8's, which say one fresh ring and integer increments. It runs on the writer's task, outside the stepping-loop invariant.
